The 2006 Red Data Book lists this plant as Tulipa affinis. The archived exact taxonomic match from GBIF treats that name as a synonym of Tulipa fosteriana. This description covers the historical national record only. It does not cover the full modern range of the accepted species. The plant has an ovoid bulb up to 4 cm across, a stem up to 30 cm tall and several broad, glaucous green, hairy leaves. The solitary large red flower has a dark spot and a narrow yellow border at the base of the tepals.

In Kyrgyzstan, the account lists the Turkestan Range, the Ak-Suu basin and the mountains east of Suluktu. The plant grows on stony soils with fine earth among junipers. The account records reproduction by seed, and the English summary places flowering in April–May. No population counts were carried out.

Collecting flowers, digging up bulbs and developing the habitat for economic use are identified as threats. Cultivation in Bishkek was considered insufficiently studied, with plants quickly dying out in cultivation. The authors recommend botanical reserves, population monitoring and a ban on collection and trade. The VU category is retained solely as a feature of the historical national record.

The bulb is ovoid and up to 4 cm across. The stem reaches 30 cm and is downy towards the top. There are three to four broadly lanceolate, glaucous green, hairy leaves up to 25 cm long. The large, solitary flower is red or crimson, with a black basal spot bordered by a narrow band of bright yellow.

The historical taxon Tulipa affinis was described from stony soils with fine earth among junipers. Cultivation records are limited to unsuccessful plantings in Bishkek. They provide no measure of viability in the wild.
The national account records reproduction by seed, and the English summary places flowering in April–May. Fruiting dates and germination data are unavailable.

The national record under the name Tulipa affinis lists the Turkestan Range, the Ak-Suu basin, the Tue-Jailoo locality and the mountains east of Suluktu. The account also mentions Nuratau and the northern slopes of the Turkestan Range outside Kyrgyzstan.
Stony soils with fine earth among junipers, according to the national account of Tulipa affinis.

Korolkov’s tulip is a brightly coloured bulbous plant whose main range, according to the national account, lies in Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. In Kyrgyzstan, it was described from the northern slopes of the Turkestan Range. Its short stem usually reaches 10–20 cm and occasionally 30 cm. The three glaucous leaves have strongly curled margins. The solitary flower is bright red and glossy inside, with a small black spot at the base. It nods in bud.

The plant grows on sandy, gravelly and stony slopes in the foothills. The Russian text records flowering in March–April, fruiting in June–July and reproduction by seed. The English summary gives April alone for flowering, so the timing needs to be checked locally. Population size in the wild is unknown.

The showy flowers are vulnerable to collection for bouquets. Ploughing and overgrazing also damage the habitat. The account records past cultivation in the botanical gardens of Tashkent and Dushanbe. The authors recommend reserves, monitoring, a ban on collecting flowers and bulbs, and limits on grazing until seeds have formed. The national category VU refers to the 2006 edition.

The ovoid bulb is 1.5–2.5 cm across, with black, leathery tunics. The stem reaches 10–20 cm, occasionally 30 cm. Three glaucous leaves have strongly curled margins. The solitary, bright red flower is up to 6 cm tall, with a small black spot at the base and yellow anthers.
Sandy, gravelly and stony slopes in the foothills. The national account notes that ploughing and overgrazing threaten the habitat and that the plants are collected for bouquets.

The Russian account records flowering in March–April, fruiting in June–July and reproduction by seed. The English summary gives April for flowering. The precise local timing needs to be checked in the field.

Historical records in Kyrgyzstan place the species on the northern slopes of the Turkestan Range. The account gives its overall range as the south-western Tien Shan and Pamir-Alay, mainly in Uzbekistan and Tajikistan.
Sandy, gravelly and stony slopes in the foothills.

The broad-stamened tulip is described in the national Red Data Book as endemic to a small area of the Alay Range. Sary-Biya Pass is the only locality given. This perennial has a short growing season and an ovoid bulb up to 2 cm across. Its hairless stem, including the flower stalk, reaches about 17 cm. The specimen described has four widely spaced leaves and two yellow flowers, with a violet tint on the outside of the outer tepals.

Flowering is recorded in June. The book explicitly states that information on fruiting, habitat, population size and cultivation is unavailable. The record from the pass was therefore not used to infer precise elevations, vegetation types, soil characteristics or coordinates. Reproductive details beyond the flowering period are also unknown.

The authors list spring grazing, flower collecting and the digging up of bulbs as threats. They recommend botanical reserves where the plant is concentrated, monitoring, and restrictions on collection and grazing. The account gives no confirmation that these measures were implemented. The historical VU category documents the assessment in the 2006 edition and gives no new assessment of the species’ current status.

The bulb is ovoid, up to 2 cm across. The hairless stem with its flower stalk is about 17 cm long. There are four widely spaced leaves, with the lower leaves bent back. The lowest is linear-lanceolate and 2 cm wide. The description records two yellow flowers with tepals about 4 cm long. The filaments broaden above the midpoint.
The source describes a bulbous geophyte with a short growing season and gives no habitat conditions. The location of the pass provides no basis for inferring its ecological preferences.
It flowers in June. The available national account gives no details on fruiting or methods of reproduction.
The historical record in the 2006 edition lists Sary-Biya Pass in the Alay Range. The exact locations of populations and their current presence remain unconfirmed.

The 2006 Red Data Book describes the quadrifolious tulip as endemic to the Inner Tien Shan. Despite its Russian name, the national description gives a range of three to seven leaves. They are glaucous, sickle-shaped, channelled and often curled, with white margins. The hairless stem reaches 3–25 cm. The plant bears one to four yellow flowers that nod in bud. The tepals have green patches and a green vein on the outside.

The species is described from stony slopes. It flowers in May during its short growing season. The account describes the capsule and explicitly states that the fruiting period is unknown. It provides neither population counts nor cultivation records. The description of the fruit gives no basis for specifying when it ripens.

The main threats are spring grazing, flower collecting and the digging up of bulbs. At the time the book was prepared, specific conservation measures were reported as yet to be developed. The authors recommended botanical reserves, monitoring, and a ban on collecting plants and grazing at sites where they grow. The national category VU remains tied to the historical edition and provides no current assessment.

The bulb is broadly ovoid, 1.5–3 cm across, with stiff brownish-black tunics. The stem reaches 3–25 cm. The three to seven leaves are glaucous, sickle-shaped and channelled. There are one to four yellow flowers. The outside of the perianth has yellow-green or green patches and a central green vein.
A bulbous plant with a short growing season on the stony slopes of the Inner Tien Shan. The national account gives no detailed elevation limits or soil characteristics.
It flowers in May. Fruiting dates are unknown, and the account does not describe methods of reproduction.
The historical national record lists the Inner Tien Shan. The material consulted contains no confirmed modern observation sites.
Stony slopes, according to the 2006 national account.

The 2006 Red Data Book describes this plant under the name Tulipa zenaidae. An exact GBIF match treats that name as a synonym of Tulipa lehmanniana. The biology and distribution below refer to the national taxon concept of zenaidae and do not automatically apply to every population of the accepted species. The plant has a short stem and a solitary, nearly sessile flower. The flower is yellow inside and red outside, with a black star-shaped marking at the base. The three large, somewhat glaucous leaves have prominent veins.

The national account lists the Kyrgyz Range and the adjoining part of southern Kazakhstan. The plant grows on slopes with fine earth and gravel in the lower mountain belt, among forb and fescue steppes and shrubs. It flowers in April–May and reproduces by seed. Attempts to introduce it into cultivation were reported as difficult. Plants quickly disappeared from the plantings and produced few seeds in Bishkek.

Unregulated spring grazing, flower collecting and the digging up of bulbs are named as threats. The authors recommended reserves, monitoring and limits on collecting plants. The reference to limited numbers in the wild gives no count. The VU category is historical. The current scope of the national listing needs expert review.

The bulb is up to 3 cm across, with black or blackish-brown tunics. The stem is usually 10–15 cm tall and reaches 40 cm in shade. The three large, oblong leaves are pale glaucous green. The solitary flower, up to 5 cm long, is yellow inside and red outside, with a black star-shaped centre.

The historical national taxon concept is associated with slopes of fine earth and gravel in the lower mountain belt, among forb and fescue steppes and shrubs. In cultivation in Bishkek, plants quickly died out and produced few seeds.

The national account records reproduction by seed in the wild and in cultivation, with flowering in April–May. For plants grown in Bishkek, it separately reports flowering in mid-April lasting 8–10 days. That timing is not applied to all wild populations.
The historical record of Tulipa zenaidae refers to the Kyrgyz Range in Kyrgyzstan and southern Kazakhstan. It gives no reconstruction of the full modern range of Tulipa lehmanniana.
Slopes with fine earth and gravel in the lower mountain belt among forb and fescue steppes and shrubs.

The national book lists this plant as Juno orchioides. The archived exact GBIF match accepts the name Iris orchioides. It is a spring perennial with a bulb about 2 cm across and fleshy, cord-like roots that persist after the above-ground parts die back. The light green, sickle-shaped leaves have whitish margins. The flowers range from pale to bright yellow and have a darker spot on the outer lobes of the perianth.

In Kyrgyzstan, the account lists the Kyrgyz and Talas Ranges. It describes suitable sites as slopes with fine earth, clay, stones or gravel from the foothills to the middle mountain belt. Growth resumes in the second half of March. Flowering begins in mid-April and lasts one to two weeks. In June the seeds ripen and the above-ground parts dry out. The plant reproduces by seed and by forming new bulbs. Seedlings first flower in their fourth or fifth year.

Collection for bouquets, digging up bulbs and trampling by livestock are named as threats. The book reports many years of successful cultivation at the botanical garden of the National Academy of Sciences of the Kyrgyz Republic and records historical protection from 1975. The authors recommend careful pasture management, a ban on collecting plants and a botanical reserve. Current population size is unconfirmed.

The stem reaches 10–30 cm and bears one flower or, more often, three to five. The bulb is about 2 cm across with dense brown tunics, and the roots are fleshy. The light green, sickle-shaped leaves have white margins. Flowers are 4.4–6 cm long and range from pale to bright yellow, with a dark spot on the outer lobes.

A spring bulbous perennial of the foothills and middle mountain belt. The national account notes that the fleshy roots persist after the above-ground parts dry out. By the time of publication, the botanical garden of the National Academy of Sciences of the Kyrgyz Republic had successfully grown the plant for more than 40 years.

Growth resumes in the second half of March, and flowering lasts one to two weeks from mid-April. The seeds ripen in June, after which the above-ground parts dry out. The plant reproduces by seed and vegetatively, forming a cluster of bulbs of different ages. Seedlings flower in their fourth or fifth year.
The 2006 national account lists the Kyrgyz and Talas Ranges. It places the overall range in the western and northern Tien Shan. The available material adds no modern observations.
Slopes with fine earth, clay, stones or gravel from the foothills to the middle mountain belt.

The national book lists this plant under two names, and the archived GBIF match confirms Iris kolpakowskiana as the accepted one. It is a short plant with an ovoid bulb in netted fibrous tunics. The stem is leafless and bears a single flower. The three basal leaves share a sheath at the base. The violet flower has a white spot on the outer lobes of the perianth and a yellow crest.

In Kyrgyzstan, the foothills of the Talas and Kyrgyz Ranges are reliably documented. The authors themselves considered the mention of the Fergana Range to require verification, so it was excluded from confirmed records. The plant grows on slopes with loess, fine earth or stones in the foothills and lower mountain belt. It flowers in March–April, fruits in May–June and reproduces by seed.

The source records loss of growing sites near settlements and recreation areas, widespread collecting for bouquets and the digging up of underground parts. It recommends assessing wild populations, managing pastures carefully, establishing a botanical reserve and banning the collection and sale of flowers. The historical VU category provides no current assessment. The photograph from Kazakhstan illustrates the species and provides no evidence of its presence in Kyrgyzstan.

The ovoid bulb is 1–1.5 cm thick and has netted fibrous tunics. The leafless stem reaches 8–20 cm and bears a single flower. There are three basal leaves. The violet flower is 4–6 cm long, with a white spot on the outer lobes and a yellow crest. The fruit is a ribbed, three-chambered capsule.

An early spring plant with a short growing season, found on slopes with loess, fine earth or stones. The book records a loss of growing sites near settlements and recreation areas. The extent of that loss has not been quantified.
The national account records reproduction by seed, flowering in March–April and fruiting in May–June. In cultivation at the Bishkek botanical garden it flowers in the first half of April.

Historical records confirm its presence in the foothills of the Talas and Kyrgyz Ranges. The original source regards its presence in the Fergana Range as unverified and excludes it from the confirmed distribution.
Slopes with loess, fine earth or stones in the foothills and lower mountain belt.

The 2006 Red Data Book lists this plant as Thesium minkwitzianum. An exact taxonomic match from GBIF accepts Chrysothesium minkwitzianum, while the national biological information remains associated with the original name. This rare relict perennial has a thick root with several crowns and numerous ribbed stems. Its leathery, dark glaucous leaves have a whitish margin. The yellowish flowers grow in many-flowered racemes, and the ribbed nutlets have a conspicuous network of veins.

In Kyrgyzstan, the account mentions only the Kumbel Range in the Chatkal Range system. Outside the country it lists the Chatkal Nature Reserve in Uzbekistan. The plant grows on stony slopes. The Russian text records flowering and fruiting in May and reproduction by seed, while the English summary describes its biology as poorly known. The discrepancies are flagged for editorial review.

Construction and mineral extraction are named as threats. The source records protection in the Besh-Aral and Chatkal nature reserves and recommends targeted population studies. The old plant counts lack survey dates and were omitted from the population size field. The CR category refers to the historical national assessment.

Numerous hairless, ribbed stems reach 40 cm and are densely leafy. The leaves are dark glaucous, leathery and broadly lanceolate, with whitish margins. The yellowish perianth is 12–15 mm long, with a five-lobed limb. The fruits are elliptical, ribbed nutlets with a pitted surface.

A rare relict perennial of stony slopes. The national account gives no details on how it obtains nutrients and does not confirm parasitism. Traits of other members of the genus are not assumed for this taxon.

The Russian text of the national account records flowering and fruiting in May and reproduction by seed. The English summary indicates that details of its biology are lacking. Germination conditions and pollinators are unknown.

In Kyrgyzstan, the national account lists the Kumbel Range in the Chatkal Range system and the Besh-Aral Nature Reserve. Outside Kyrgyzstan, it lists the Chatkal Nature Reserve in Uzbekistan. Current presence remains unconfirmed.
Stony slopes.

The great white pelican is listed in the 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan as Pelecanus onocrotalus. The account describes it as an occasional passage migrant through the country and reports autumn sightings and some instances of wintering in the Chüy Valley. These historical reports establish neither current population size nor a confirmed present-day range. Individual birds were observed on passage.

The habitat described consists of large bodies of water with dense reedbeds. The bird feeds on fish. The account also describes the species’ general colonial breeding biology, including nests on islands and mats of broken reeds, small clutches and lengthy incubation. These details provide no evidence of breeding in Kyrgyzstan, so the local reproduction field is left blank.

Access to large bodies of water for resting is important during migration. Threats listed include changes to the water regime, pollution, reedbed burning, declining fish stocks and poaching. The authors propose seasonal protection of important sites and designation of key areas for birds. The recommendation provides no evidence that such areas have already been established. The national assessment of Near Threatened is retained with the date of the historical edition and is omitted from the global IUCN field.
The national book describes rare autumn passage through the Chüy Valley and occasional wintering in Kyrgyzstan.
The national account explicitly describes a diet of fish.
The historical national records refer to autumn passage through the Chüy Valley. The material consulted does not establish the present-day distribution.
Large bodies of water with dense reedbeds.

The pygmy cormorant is listed in the 2006 edition as Phalacrocorax pygmaeus. The archived GBIF response confirms it as a synonym of the accepted name Microcarbo pygmaeus, at the same taxonomic rank and with the same authorship. The catalogue entry uses the accepted name, while the national listing and descriptions remain linked to the historical name.

The account reports passage mainly through the Chüy Valley and winter sightings near Bishkek. Possible breeding in the area west of Issyk-Kul remained conjectural. Fish-rich wetlands are important, as the birds catch prey by diving and swimming underwater. The account mentions group fishing and resting with wings spread out to dry.

Sightings of flocks in 2005 and of two birds in January 2006 document encounters and provide no estimate of the overall population. The book identifies declining fish stocks and direct killing as the main threats. It recommends protecting feeding and resting sites. The general description of nests and clutches provides no evidence of local breeding. The historical reference to IUCN is not used as a current global status.
The national account records migration and wintering. Birds may fish in groups and rest on the shore with their wings spread.
The source records a diet of fish, caught by diving and swimming underwater.
Historical records relate mainly to the Chüy Valley. Breeding west of Issyk-Kul was only suspected.
Fish-rich wetlands.

The 2006 national edition lists the lesser kestrel as Falco naumanni. The account places it in the lower and middle mountain belts and records sightings in the south-west of the country, the Issyk-Kul basin and some inland valleys. The bird prefers trees and shrubs on river floodplains and slopes, though it also uses cultivated landscapes.

The source lists mouse-like rodents, lizards and large insects, especially beetles, among its prey. The authors give no details on breeding biology in Kyrgyzstan. A dated sighting of young birds in Boom Gorge and an old local density figure provide no current estimate of the entire population. Breeding and population size remain unknown in the structured fields.

Nest destruction and illegal shooting are named as threats. The book suggests possible competition with the common kestrel, but this is not treated as an established cause of decline. The authors recommend locating and protecting nesting sites, designating locally protected areas, conducting annual surveys and informing residents. The national category Vulnerable dates from 2006 and provides no basis for inferring the current global status.
The historical account records sightings up to 2500 m. It gives no description of local breeding biology.
Mouse-like rodents, lizards and large insects, especially beetles.
Historical records come from the Arstanbap area, Karkyra, the Naryn floodplain and the Issyk-Kul basin. The current range has not been updated.
Lower and middle mountain belts with trees and shrubs on floodplains and slopes, as well as cultivated landscapes.

The 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan lists the gyrfalcon as Falco rusticolus. The national account describes it as a rare winter visitor, with historical sightings in the Chüy Valley, around Issyk-Kul and in the Naryn region. High mountain areas and foothill valleys are listed as sites used in the country. The account gives an Arctic breeding range, which is not applied to Kyrgyzstan here.

The source reports a single sighting in Baibiche-Too Gorge in November 2002 and gives no estimate of the national population. The account describes the clutch, incubation and chick development as general features of the species. They give no evidence of local breeding, which the book recommends investigating. Diet and identifying features are not described separately in the account and are recorded as unknown.

Capture for falconry and nest destruction are named as limiting factors. The authors propose public outreach and protection of any breeding sites found. These are proposals, with no record of programmes having been carried out. The historical national category Least Concern does not represent a current global IUCN assessment or change the fact that winter sightings in the country are rare.
The national account records the species as a visitor in some winters. The material consulted does not confirm local breeding.
Historical sightings come from the Chüy Valley, the Issyk-Kul area and Baibiche-Too. Present-day occurrence was not established.
The book lists high mountain areas and foothill valleys for Kyrgyzstan.

The 2006 national book lists the osprey as Pandion haliaetus. The account brings together historical sightings at waters in the Chüy Valley, at Issyk-Kul and along the At-Bashy River. It describes clear, fish-rich waters with wooded banks. These details describe the conditions in which the bird uses the area, and its current presence still needs to be checked.

The source reports old sightings of pairs during the breeding season and records of nests near Sary-Chelek. The Kyrgyz and Russian versions give different years for the nest records, and no survey of current breeding was carried out for this batch of records. Local breeding is therefore left unconfirmed. The book gives March–April for spring arrival and late August to October for autumn migration.

Development of water bodies, felling of bankside trees, declining fish stocks, disturbance and nest destruction are named as threats. The authors propose carrying out counts, locating and protecting nesting sites, and investigating the use of artificial nest sites. The account gives no direct description of the diet or detailed identification features. These fields were left blank because general knowledge of the species is insufficient for filling them in.
The historical account places arrival in March–April and autumn migration between the last third of August and October.
Historical records come from the Chüy Valley, Issyk-Kul, along the At-Bashy River and near Sary-Chelek. Current breeding is unconfirmed.
Clear, fish-rich waters with wooded banks.

The 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan lists Pallas’s fish eagle as Haliaeetus leucoryphus. The national account describes it as a rare passage migrant and winter visitor. Old published reports of summer sightings confirm neither breeding nor current nesting. The catalogue entry preserves the distinction between a sighting and evidence of an established breeding population.

The habitats listed are bodies of water with extensive reedbeds and river floodplains with poplars and willows. The authors give no reliable population data, as no dedicated counts were carried out. The account provides no detailed description of appearance, diet or local breeding biology, so those fields remain blank.

Direct killing and loss of suitable habitat are named as the main threats. The authors recommend protecting wintering sites, estimating population size, studying limiting factors and informing residents. The proposal for a breeding centre is recorded as a historical recommendation. The national category Vulnerable refers to the 2006 book, and the current legal status of the international agreements mentioned at the time has not been verified.
The book describes a rare passage migrant and winter visitor. Old published summer sightings do not confirm breeding.
The historical national account describes passage and wintering in Kyrgyzstan. Present-day sites have not been established.
Bodies of water with reedbeds and river floodplains with poplar and willow woodland.

The 2006 national edition lists the white-tailed eagle as Haliaeetus albicilla. The account associates its wintering with the Chüy Valley, Issyk-Kul and waters in the south of the country. Riverbanks and lakeshores need to offer feeding opportunities, while tall trees and cliffs are mentioned in the general description of the species’ habitat. This provides no evidence of local breeding.

The Russian and English versions give different numbers of wintering birds, and no year is given for the overall estimate. Those figures remain in the source account and were omitted from the national population size field. The general details of the clutch and incubation are not used as evidence of breeding in Kyrgyzstan, where the source describes the species as a winter visitor. The account gives no detailed identification features or direct description of diet.

Shoreline development, food shortages and direct killing are named as limiting factors. The authors recommend protecting wintering sites, carrying out counts and informing the public. Mentions of the hunting ban and international appendices reflect the situation at the time of publication and have not been checked against current law. The historical national category Near Threatened is kept separate from the current global assessment, which remains unknown here.
The 2006 national account describes the species as present in Kyrgyzstan in winter.
Historical wintering records come from waters in the Chüy Valley, at Issyk-Kul and in southern Kyrgyzstan. No current data were added.
Shorelines with fish and waterbirds. The general habitat description also mentions tall trees and cliffs.

The 2006 book and the archived 2009 list record the Russian Rossomyrmex as Rossomyrmex proformicarum. The exact GBIF response confirms the accepted species name. The historical national account describes extremely rare records in the eastern Chüy Valley. These records establish neither confirmed modern sightings nor a current population estimate.

The worker ants are slender, with a yellowish-red head and thorax and a predominantly black abdomen. The habitat is associated with unploughed steppe soils and colonies of ants of the genus Proformica. The account describes social parasitism: the ants raid host nests and carry away pupae. Much of the species’ biology remained unstudied. The suggestion of mainly nocturnal activity is treated as a hypothesis.

Conservation depends on keeping the steppe community intact, including the host ants. The national account lists ploughing, overgrazing, land improvement and pesticide contamination. The authors propose searching for other colonies, preserving unploughed sites and establishing small protected areas. Diet and reproductive details remain unknown because general information about ants provides no basis for filling in these fields.

According to the book, workers are 5.2–5.6 mm long. The head, thorax and petiole are yellowish red, and the abdomen is black with a slight bronze sheen. Males and females were not described in the 2006 account.
The national account describes a social parasite of Proformica. In raids, workers carry pupae away from host nests. The full life cycle is poorly understood.
Historical records in Kyrgyzstan come from the eastern Chüy Valley near Orlovka. No new observations or coordinates were added.
Unploughed steppe with ground nests of Proformica. The historical national record comes from the foothills at about 1150 m.

The 2006 national book lists the Aral barbel as Barbus brachycephalus. The accepted combination Luciobarbus brachycephalus is confirmed by an exact synonym match from GBIF. The species also appears on the 2009 list. The book reports its disappearance from Kyrgyzstan, a historical conclusion from the source. Its status has not been reassessed for the current year.

The account describes a large silvery fish with a darker back and grey paired fins. Historical local records come from lowland stretches of the Chu and connected channels. The barbel fed near the riverbed, and the account lists molluscs, insect larvae and young fish. Spawning is described from late April to early June. This information does not confirm current breeding in the river.

The authors cite the dam at the Tashatkul Reservoir and fishing during the spawning season among the causes of disappearance. The proposal for reintroduction requires biological justification and carries no recommendation to release fish. Current population size remains unknown. The historical national category, accepted nomenclature and present-day occurrence have different evidential bases and are kept separate.
The national account describes a silvery body with a dark back that gradually lightens towards the belly. The paired fins are grey, and the fish reaches 90 cm in length.
The book describes past spawning migrations along the Chu and a subsequent return downstream. Current occurrence is unconfirmed.
The national account lists bottom-dwelling invertebrates, including molluscs and insect larvae, as well as young fish.
The 2006 book gives late April to early June for spawning and reports sexual maturity from four years of age. These historical details provide no evidence of current spawning in Kyrgyzstan.
Historically known from the Chu in Kyrgyzstan, the species was reported to have disappeared in the 2006 book. Current presence has not been established.
Historically, lowland stretches of rivers, the lower Chu, channels and lakes with throughflow.

The 2006 national book lists Gypsophila-like allochrusa as Allochrusa gypsophiloides and also gives Acanthophyllum gypsophiloides as an alternative name. The 2009 list uses Acanthophyllum, the accepted name confirmed by an exact synonym match from GBIF. The link between these names gives no basis for transferring information from a similar-looking plant.

This perennial has a thick vertical root and highly branched stems that form rounded clumps. It has narrow leaves and many-flowered panicles with white or pinkish petals. The national account describes the habitat as savanna-like vegetation. Historical records in Kyrgyzstan come from the Chatkal, Talas and Pskem Ranges. The plant is reported to flower from June to August, fruit in August and September, and reproduce by seed.

Land development and root harvesting are the main threats recorded. The book associates the plant’s use with saponins in its roots. The catalogue entry makes no recommendation to collect it or use it medicinally. The authors propose strengthening protection in the Besh-Aral Nature Reserve and investigating cultivation. The material consulted contains no current quantitative population assessment.

A perennial with a thick vertical root. The branched flowering stems reach 70 cm and often form rounded clumps. The leaves are narrow, and the flowers are borne in panicles with white or pinkish petals.
The book describes a perennial forming rounded, branched clumps. It gives no further information on interactions with other organisms.
According to the national account, it flowers from June to August, fruits from August to September and reproduces by seed.
The 2006 edition lists the Chatkal, Talas and Pskem Ranges in Kyrgyzstan. No current records were added.
Savanna-like vegetation in the historically recorded mountain areas.

The 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan lists the false hooked fumitory as Corydalis pseudoadunca. The same species name appears in the 2009 list and is confirmed by the exact taxonomic response from GBIF. The national account describes it as endemic to the Pamir-Alay. A separate modern survey would be needed to assess its populations today.

It is a perennial herb with sturdy stems and repeatedly divided leaves. The flowers are borne in fairly long, dense racemes, and the corolla has a short, straight, blunt spur. The narrow, oblong fruits hang downwards. The account associates the plant with stony slopes, gravelly bluffs and riverbanks from the middle to the upper mountain belt. It records flowering and fruiting from June to August and reproduction by seed.

The account explicitly gives no information on population size, limiting factors or cultivation. The threats field was therefore left blank instead of being filled with a standard list of grazing, collecting or construction. The authors chiefly recommend studying its population size and biology and establishing a botanical reserve where it is concentrated. The historical category VU is retained with the year, and no global IUCN category or current national status is assigned.

The book describes a perennial with sturdy stems 20–40 cm tall and leaves divided almost three times pinnately. The racemes are dense. The corolla is about 15 mm long with a short, straight, blunt spur, and the fruits are long and narrow.
The national account records flowering and fruiting from June to August and reproduction by seed.
The historical account lists the Alay and Trans-Alay Ranges, including Taldyk and the upper Kyzyl-Suu. No modern locality records were added.
Stony slopes, gravelly bluffs and riverbanks from the middle to the upper mountain belt.

The 2006 book and the 2009 list record microfumitory as Fumariola turkestanica. The exact GBIF response confirms the accepted species name. The national account places the historical localities in the foothills of the north-western Alay Range, in the Shakhimardan and Isfairamsai basins. No unverified modern localities were added.

It is a short annual with divided leaves on slender stalks and small clusters of yellow flowers. The fruit is described as a single-seeded nutlet that darkens as it ripens. An annual 6–10 cm tall with divided leaves on slender stalks, yellow flowers and single-seeded nutlets that turn black when ripe.

This annual reproduces by seed. The account records no vegetative reproduction. No precise dates were chosen from the differing Russian and English versions.

Historical records come from the basins of the Shakhimardan and Isfairamsai rivers and the land between them, in Kyrgyzstan and the Uzbek enclave. The authors reject the erroneous record for Tajikistan.
Cracks in steeply inclined or sheer limestone cliffs, mainly facing north-east, and occasionally at the foot of cliffs. The historical account gives 1050–1500 m.

The 2006 national book lists Litvinov’s rosewort as Rhodiola litwinowii. The same name appears in the 2009 list and has an exact match to an accepted name in GBIF. This perennial has a stout rhizome with several crowns and numerous short, leafy stems. The book records stony and gravelly soils and loose rock in the upper mountain belt, including passes and sites near glaciers. Flowering is recorded in June–July, fruiting in July–August and reproduction by seed. The account reports declining numbers and links the pressure to economic activity. No conjectural medicinal properties or new locality records were added.

A perennial herb with a stout rhizome and several crowns. The numerous stems are 10–17 cm tall and densely leafy. The leaves are flat and alternate, with uneven teeth. The inflorescence is dense and many-flowered.
The book records flowering in June–July, fruiting in July–August and reproduction by seed.
The historical account lists the Kyrgyz, Talas, Chatkal, Fergana, Alay and Turkestan Ranges. Current records are unavailable.
Stony and gravelly soils and loose rock in the upper mountain belt, including sites near glaciers and passes.

The 2006 book and the 2009 list record the Tien Shan sibiraea as Sibiraea tianschanica. The archived GBIF response gives an exact match to this accepted name. The national account describes the plant as a rare shrub of the northern Tien Shan. It is a low shrub with dark brown stems and narrow, lanceolate, sessile leaves. Its small flowers are borne in racemes grouped into a panicle. The account places it in the upper mountain belt, in thickets of shrubs and prostrate juniper, glades in open spruce woodland, and subalpine and alpine meadows. A low shrub up to 0.5 m tall, with thick dark brown stems and narrow, lanceolate, sessile leaves. The small flowers are borne in racemes and panicles.

Upper mountain belt, in thickets of shrubs and prostrate juniper, glades in open spruce woodland, and subalpine and alpine meadows.

The snow pigeon is a high mountain bird. The 2006 account gives specific historical records from the eastern Alay Valley.

Rocky highlands above 3000 m. The nest described in the Russian account was on a rock ledge.

National sightings are few and localised. They establish neither current population size nor permanent occupation of all potentially suitable areas.

The Russian text describes a nest found near Nura on 14 June 1985 that contained 2 eggs. It was made of grass rootlets. The source only suggests that the nest may have been reused.

The historical national record comes from the eastern Alay Valley. The overall range in the account includes the Pamir-Alay, the Himalayas and Tibet.

The authors propose studying its distribution, numbers and biology in likely habitats.

The national category and the sightings described come from the historical 2006 edition. Current population size has not been established. Current legal status and present-day occurrence need separate confirmation.
National sightings are few and localised. They establish neither current population size nor permanent occupation of all potentially suitable areas.
The Russian text describes a nest found near Nura on 14 June 1985 that contained 2 eggs. It was made of grass rootlets. The source only suggests that the nest may have been reused.
The historical national record comes from the eastern Alay Valley. The overall range in the account includes the Pamir-Alay, the Himalayas and Tibet.
Rocky highlands above 3000 m. The nest described in the Russian account was on a rock ledge.

The yellow-eyed pigeon occurs mainly in Central Asia. In Kyrgyzstan it was historically associated with river valleys in the lower mountain belt.

River bluffs in valleys in the lower mountain belt. The account also mentions tree cavities and abandoned buildings.

The account places autumn departure in August–September. Old reports of passage in large numbers are not used as a current estimate.

Seeds of wild plants and cultivated cereals.

The clutch contains 2 eggs. Both parents feed the young. The account suggests that two broods in one summer are possible.

Historical records come from the Chüy and Talas Valleys and the area around Fergana, including river bluffs along the Chu, Ak-Su and Kök-Art.

Hunting at nesting sites and during passage, and destruction of nest sites.

The authors recommend determining the current distribution and population size and developing conservation measures.

The national category and the sightings described come from the historical 2006 edition. Current population size has not been established. Current legal status and present-day occurrence need separate confirmation.
The account places autumn departure in August–September. Old reports of passage in large numbers are not used as a current estimate.
Seeds of wild plants and cultivated cereals.
The clutch contains 2 eggs. Both parents feed the young. The account suggests that two broods in one summer are possible.
Historical records come from the Chüy and Talas Valleys and the area around Fergana, including river bluffs along the Chu, Ak-Su and Kök-Art.
River bluffs in valleys in the lower mountain belt. The account also mentions tree cavities and abandoned buildings.

The Eurasian eagle-owl is a mainly resident bird of prey of mountain landscapes, covered in the 2006 national edition.

Mountain woodland with cliffs, clay bluffs and caves. In winter it may descend into valleys between the mountains and approach settlements.

It makes short movements between elevations and may winter high in the mountains when food is plentiful. The account notes how much local birds depend on prey availability.

Mammals, including hares, mice and voles, and less often birds.

In mountain areas, the account gives April for laying, usually with 2–5 eggs. The female incubates for 33–35 days. The young remain at the nesting site for a long time.

Historical records cover the Issyk-Kul area, inland valleys and the Kyrgyz, Alay and Chatkal Ranges. Breeding at some sites is only suspected.

Taking birds for their feathers.

Deaths on power lines and roads.

Declines in prey populations.

The authors propose public outreach. The account also discusses captive breeding and collecting feathers from live birds as a recommendation.

The national category and the sightings described come from the historical 2006 edition. Current population size has not been established. Current legal status and present-day occurrence need separate confirmation.
It makes short movements between elevations and may winter high in the mountains when food is plentiful. The account notes how much local birds depend on prey availability.
Mammals, including hares, mice and voles, and less often birds.
In mountain areas, the account gives April for laying, usually with 2–5 eggs. The female incubates for 33–35 days. The young remain at the nesting site for a long time.
Historical records cover the Issyk-Kul area, inland valleys and the Kyrgyz, Alay and Chatkal Ranges. Breeding at some sites is only suspected.
Mountain woodland with cliffs, clay bluffs and caves. In winter it may descend into valleys between the mountains and approach settlements.

The goitered gazelle is a member of the bovid family, listed in the 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan under category CR. This category belongs to the historical national account and does not provide a new assessment of the species. The book uses the spelling Gazella subgutturoza. The 2009 version of the statutory list gives Gazella subgutturosa, which matches the accepted name in GBIF and the Mammal Diversity Database. The account associates the former distribution in the country with the Issyk-Kul area, Orto-Tokoy and Leilek District. The records from the 1930s–1970s do not establish present-day occurrence. The habitat is described as open gravel and clay deserts. It feeds mainly in the morning and evening. Poaching and land development in suitable areas are the main threats identified by the national source. The discussion of restoring the population in Kyrgyzstan at a scientific seminar in 2026 provides neither a survey result nor confirmation of successful reintroduction. A reliable current estimate of the national population is unavailable, so the population size remains unknown.

According to the national account, it is mainly resident and feeds in the morning and evening. In dry habitats it uses available water sources and pools that collect after rain or snowmelt. These details do not replace current local studies.

The account gives general reproductive details. Gestation lasts about 5.5–6 months, and females usually have 1–2 young. The rutting season is described using material from Kazakhstan and is not assumed to apply to an unconfirmed present-day population in Kyrgyzstan.

Historical records in the 2006 Red Data Book cover the Issyk-Kul area, Orto-Tokoy and Leilek District. The account itself does not confirm that the species was still present at the time of publication. The current Mammal Diversity Database lists Kyrgyzstan, which does not confirm that the animals are present at any specific site today. No present-day localities or range boundaries are assigned for Kyrgyzstan.

The 2006 national account describes open, flat or hilly areas of gravel and clay deserts with sparse herbaceous vegetation. This is a description of historical habitat and does not map a current population.

The white-winged woodpecker is a member of the woodpecker family with its own account in the 2006 Red Data Book of the Kyrgyz Republic. The national category in that edition is LC. This historical national listing is separate from any new legal or global conservation decision. The accepted scientific name Dendrocopos leucopterus is confirmed by an exact species match from GBIF and by an ITIS record. The book gives 1870 as the year of authorship, while current taxonomic databases give 1871. The discrepancy is retained in the research material and is not used to create a separate taxon. The national account describes a resident bird of deciduous woodland, chiefly the walnut-fruit forests in the south. It also mentions floodplain forests along the Naryn and At-Bashy and the Alay and Fergana Ranges. The bird nests in cavities and feeds mainly on insects, as well as nuts and fruit. Its breeding biology is incompletely known. The account contains no systematic national population assessment. The main threat recorded is uncontrolled felling of old trees, which reduces the number of suitable nesting sites.
A resident species that nests in cavities in deciduous trees. Old trees with suitable cavities are essential for maintaining nesting sites.
According to the national account, it feeds chiefly on insects, including those that damage forests. It also eats nut kernels and fruit from wild plants that bear stone fruit.

The account describes the nesting information as fragmentary. The nest is in a cavity, and young birds were recorded in mid-July. The source does not establish laying dates, clutch size or incubation length.

The 2006 national account records walnut-fruit forests in southern Kyrgyzstan, with occasional records from the Naryn and At-Bashy floodplains, the Alay and Fergana Ranges and Bishkek. These details come from a specific historical source. No new sightings or current population estimates were added.

Deciduous, walnut-fruit and floodplain forests. The 2006 national account records occurrence up to 2800 m above sea level. This historical record does not establish the species’ current upper elevation limit.

The Persian rowan is a tree in the rose family with its own account in the second edition of the Red Data Book of the Kyrgyz Republic. The historical name Sorbus persica corresponds to the accepted combination Hedlundia persica. The change of genus refers to the same species. POWO confirms that these names are homotypic synonyms.

The 2006 account describes a tree with simple leathery leaves, white flowers and orange-red fruit. It lists several mountain ranges in Kyrgyzstan, but the authors specifically cautioned that some localities were known only from herbarium specimens. The list therefore does not confirm that populations survive in these areas.

The main pressures named are felling for craft wood and poor natural regeneration. Cultivation at the botanical garden was described as unsuccessful, with stunted plants that did not flower. The book recommended finding, counting and protecting surviving trees and establishing a botanical reserve along the middle reaches of the Kögart. These are historical proposals whose implementation was not established during preparation of this entry.

The national category VU belongs to the 2006 edition. Current population size, the condition of the localities and the version of the list currently in force remain unconfirmed. The entry was prepared for educational use and is awaiting independent scientific review.

According to the 2006 account, the tree reaches 5 m. The leaves are simple, elliptical or elongate-elliptical, shallowly lobed and covered in white felt-like hairs underneath. They are 5–8 cm long. The petals are white, and the fruits are orange-red with a slightly glaucous bloom.
The book notes poor regeneration. The Russian account describes detailed biology as unstudied. The experience of cultivation in Bishkek is not generalised to wild populations.
The English summary of the 2006 account reports flowering in May, fruiting in September and reproduction by seed, with very poor regeneration. These details come from the historical source.

The book lists the Talas, Kyrgyz, Uzun-Akhmat and Fergana Ranges, Kokiyirim and Western Ak-Shyirak. Even at the time, some localities were known only from herbarium specimens. Current occurrence has not been verified.
Mountain gorges, according to historical records in the 2006 Red Data Book.

Petunnikov’s almond is a small shrub in the rose family. The 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan lists it as Amygdalus petunnikowii, a relict species with a restricted range in the western Tien Shan. POWO links this name and the current combination Prunus petunnikowii as homotypic synonyms for the same species.

The national account describes spineless branches, narrow leaves, pink flowers and densely hairy fruits. The plant grows on north-facing gravelly slopes in the belt of trees and shrubs. In Kyrgyzstan, the account lists the Chatkal basin and the western part of the Talas Range. These records document the historical range. Current distribution would require a new survey.

The book records reproduction by seed and almost no self-seeding in the wild. Overgrazing is named as a significant limiting factor. It mentions cultivation at the botanical garden since 1965. The occasional damage in years with sharp winter temperature changes concerns cultivated plants.

For conservation, the authors proposed botanical reserves where the species is concentrated and further introduction into cultivation. The VU category is given with the historical year 2006. The account does not establish population size, and no new national estimates were obtained for this entry. The field remains unknown.

A shrub up to 1 m tall, with hairless, spineless branches. The leaves are narrowly lanceolate and usually 2–3 cm long. The flowers are pink. The fruit is asymmetrical, with a densely hairy, reddish-brown pericarp.
The historical account describes a relict shrub with almost no natural self-seeding. The current viability of its populations has not been assessed.
According to the book, it flowers in mid-April, and the fruits ripen in September. It reproduces by seed. The near absence of self-seeding comes from observations summarised in 2006.

Historical records come from the Chatkal Range, the Chatkal basin and the western Talas Range. Outside the country, it is recorded in the western Tien Shan of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. Current records are unconfirmed.
North-facing gravelly slopes among trees and shrubs in the western Tien Shan, according to the 2006 book.

Turkestan kosopoljanskia is a perennial umbellifer historically listed in the national Red Data Book as Kosopoljanskia turkestanica. The current combination Schrenkia turkestanica is supported by GBIF and a regional taxonomic treatment from 2022. The treatment links the two names and lists Kyrgyzstan, including the Talas area.

The 2006 account describes glaucous, hairless stems, divided leaves and compound umbels. The plant was recorded on dry shale scree, stony and conglomerate slopes, and variegated salt-bearing clays. This list reports the substrates given in the national source. It is not used to calculate the area of the current range.

The book records flowering in June, fruiting in July and reproduction by seed. The authors suggest that rainwater could wash the fruits into hot foothills and that this could limit the species. The entry retains this as a hypothesis, with no claim that it is a proven cause of decline.

Historical recommendations included searching for new localities and establishing botanical reserves. There are no confirmed modern counts or records showing that the measures were carried out. The national category VU refers to 2006 and does not stand in for a global assessment or the statutory list in force in 2026.

According to the 2006 description, the plant is 40–60 cm tall, with a cylindrical taproot and one or 2–3 branching, hairless, glaucous stems. The leaves are mostly basal and twice pinnately divided. The hairless, ovoid fruits split into two mericarps.
The book suggests that ripe fruits may be washed into unsuitable hot foothills. A causal link has not been established, and the material contains no modern ecological studies.
According to the 2006 account, it flowers in June, fruits in July and reproduces by seed.

Historical records come from the upper Talas, Ortok-Too, Uch-Bulak, the Alay Range in the Ak-Buura Valley, and the Jumgal Valley near the Kökömeren. These sites are not treated as confirmed locations of present-day populations.
Dry shale scree, slopes of stone and fine earth, conglomerate slopes and variegated salt-bearing clays.

Anomalous alajja is a rhizomatous perennial in the mint family. The national Red Data Book describes it under two historical generic combinations, Alajja anomala and Erianthera anomala. A 2011 paper by Sennikov and colleagues documents the combination Eriophyton anomalum and herbarium specimens from Kyrgyzstan. Together with the exact match from GBIF, this supports using the current name in a single entry covering the synonyms.

Dense felt-like hairs and large violet-pink flowers give the plant its distinctive appearance. The national account associates it with steep, stony, south-facing slopes and scree in the alpine and subnival belts. The Inner Tien Shan and the Alay Range are listed for Kyrgyzstan. These details summarise historical finds.

The book places flowering in July–August and gives both seed and vegetative reproduction as possible. There is no quantitative population estimate, and specific limiting factors have not been identified. The general description of rarity therefore provides neither an estimate in numbers nor evidence of decline.

In 2006, the authors listed no specific conservation measures and recommended preserving high mountain habitats. The VU category is given only with the source year. Current information on populations, sites where they survive and the effectiveness of protection needs separate verification. Scientific review of this entry remains pending.

A rhizomatous perennial with dense, velvety, felt-like hairs that give it a greyish appearance. The flowers are borne 2–4 to a false whorl. The corolla is violet-pink, two-lipped and 3–4 cm long, with soft hairs on the outside.
The historical account describes a high mountain species. It identifies no specific limiting factors.
According to the 2006 book, it flowers in July–August and reproduces by seed and vegetatively.
The Inner Tien Shan, including Toguz-Toro and Mount Ak-Teke, and the Alay Range. The 2006 national account and the 2011 taxonomic paper do not represent current monitoring.
Steep, stony, south-facing slopes and scree in the alpine and subnival belts.

The 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan treats Schennikov’s otostegia as a distinct rare subshrub. Current GBIF and POWO records link the name Otostegia schennikovii to Moluccella olgae. POWO treats the names as heterotypic synonyms, with the national name and the accepted name based on different types. The historical description therefore cannot automatically be applied to all populations of Moluccella olgae as more broadly defined.

The name, morphology, ecology and localities in this entry refer to the national concept of O. schennikovii. The account describes low-growing plants with fleshy opposite leaves and pale cream flowers. They occur on south-facing slopes with outcrops of variegated rock. The book lists several widely separated areas. These records do not establish the current condition of populations.

The Russian text records flowering in June–July, fruiting in July–August and reproduction by seed. Heavy grazing is the main pressure identified. The authors proposed a botanical reserve and a cultivation trial at the botanical garden. It has not been established whether these measures were carried out or what their outcome was.

The VU category is retained as the historical category in the account and does not assess the whole accepted species today. No confirmed quantitative estimate is available. The limits of this taxon concept need independent scientific review. The entry makes no new claims about current distribution.

The historical O. schennikovii is described as a low subshrub with grey, crooked lower branches, hairy young shoots 6–10 cm long and fleshy, opposite, ovoid leaves. The corolla is pale cream, and the calyx is large and two-lipped.
Widely separated historical localities of O. schennikovii. These characteristics are not assumed to apply to all populations of Moluccella olgae.
For O. schennikovii, the 2006 Russian account records flowering in June–July, fruiting in July–August and reproduction by seed. The English summary gives only July for flowering.

The historical Russian account lists the southern slopes of Western Ak-Shyirak and the Karagaty ravine, south-western Moldo-Too and the Chatkal Range near Shekaftar. The English summary gives different details for Karagaty and the slopes. No new precise coordinates are assigned.
For the national concept of O. schennikovii, south-facing slopes with outcrops of variegated rock.

Vvedensky’s sage is a perennial in the mint family with its own account in the 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan. The national spelling Salvia vvedenskyi E. Nikit. was checked against Salvia vvedenskii Nikitina, published in the Flora of the Kirghiz SSR in 1962. POWO and a separate exact GBIF query confirm the accepted name. The initial approximate match was insufficient on its own for inclusion.

The plant has divided leaves, hairy stems and large, pinkish, two-lipped flowers. The book describes it as a species with a restricted range, associated with stony slopes and slopes with fine earth in the middle mountain belt. Historical records are concentrated around the Suusamyr Range and Ketmen-Töbö basin, including near the Chichkan.

Flowering and fruiting take place in summer, and the account records reproduction by seed. The authors regarded land development as the principal threat. The material contains no counts from which to estimate present-day population size or its rate of change. The historical reference to the species’ restricted occurrence was not converted to a numerical estimate.

In 2006, the authors recommended studying the range and population status and establishing a botanical reserve on the left bank of the Chichkan. Implementation has not been verified. The VU category is tied to the 2006 edition. The entry retains verified: false and is awaiting independent scientific review.

According to the Russian account from 2006, this perennial has a densely hairy stem 40–60 cm tall. The basal leaves have long stalks, measure up to 8 × 4 cm and are pinnately divided. The corolla is pinkish and up to 35 mm long. The calyx has glandular hairs and enlarges in fruit. The Kyrgyz version gives a height of up to 65 cm. The ranges are kept separate.
The historical account describes the plant as a species with a restricted range in Kyrgyzstan. Data on cultivation and current population dynamics are unavailable.
According to the book, it flowers in June–July, fruits in July–August and reproduces by seed.
Historical records come from the Suusamyr Range, the Ketmen-Töbö basin between the Terek and Sogot-Suu, and the left bank of the Chichkan. It is unknown whether these localities survive.
Stony slopes and slopes with fine earth in the middle mountain belt, according to the 2006 national source.

The 2006 national Red Data Book lists Brandt’s hedgehog as Hemiechinus (Paraechinus) hypomelas (Brandt, 1836). The archived taxonomy gives an exact match to the current combination Paraechinus hypomelas. The species has its own historical national account. Its present-day occurrence has not been established during preparation of this entry.

The book reports one specimen and skull remains from pellets in the south of the country in 1990. The account mentions the foothills of Osh, Batken and Jalal-Abad Regions as possible sites. These records therefore do not provide a map of confirmed current populations. The current Mammal Diversity Database omits Kyrgyzstan from its country list. This limits the comparison and does not in itself invalidate the historical account.

The book summarises the literature on the species’ general biology, including nocturnal activity, use of burrows and a mixed diet. Its reproductive details are kept separate from local field observations. Population size in Kyrgyzstan is unknown.

The historical source lists ploughing, irrigation and development of previously uncultivated land as pressures. Captive breeding and micro-reserves remain proposals from 2006. The national category DD refers to that edition. The earlier deferral owing to a lack of current information remains recorded as a caveat now that the entry has been admitted.

The labelled photograph of Paraechinus hypomelas from Mushrif Park in Dubai shows dark spines, a lighter face and prominent rounded ears. This describes the photograph only. It does not establish diagnostic features or dimensions.

The 2006 book summarises the literature, describing nocturnal activity, an active season from March to October and the use of rodent burrows for shelter and wintering. It describes the species’ biology in Kyrgyzstan as unstudied.
The national account summarises published information on a diet of insects, reptiles and plant fruits. No local quantitative data on diet are available.

The book summarises published records of mating in March–April and litters of 2–5 young in May. The local breeding cycle has not been established, and the species’ biology in Kyrgyzstan remains unstudied.

The historical account reports a find in 1990 in southern Kyrgyzstan and suggests that the species inhabits the southern foothills. The current MDD country list omits Kyrgyzstan, and present-day occurrence remains unconfirmed.
Foothill steppes, semi-deserts and oases, according to the historical account. Current occupancy of particular sites in Kyrgyzstan has not been established.

Severtzov’s jerboa is a rodent with its own account in the 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan and an entry on the national list. The accepted species name Allactaga severtzovi is confirmed by an exact archived GBIF record and the current Mammal Diversity Database. The original description in 1925 used the combination Alactaga severtzovi, an earlier name for the same species.

The national account associates the species with relatively flat semi-desert, ephemeral vegetation and clay ground. Its overall range includes areas of Central Asia, the western and northern Tien Shan and the western Fergana Valley. The material does not confirm any modern records in Kyrgyzstan. The current MDD country list omits Kyrgyzstan, a discrepancy that remains unresolved. Its range in neighbouring countries cannot be used to infer local presence.

The book summarises published information on twilight and nocturnal activity, seasonal cycles and shallow burrows. Reproductive details, including records from the Kyzylkum Desert, are kept separate from local observations. Counts along survey routes in Kazakhstan are likewise not used to estimate the Kyrgyz population.

The historical category is recorded as VII, LR/lc. It has not been converted into a current code for nationalRedBook.category without direct evidence. The book recommends protecting habitats, and no specific threats have been established. The entry documents the historical listing, with population size marked unknown and scientific review marked pending.

The documented photograph of Allactaga severtzovi from Navoi Region in Uzbekistan shows long hind legs, large ears and a long tail with a contrasting tuft at the tip. This describes the illustration only and provides neither a diagnostic key nor a field record from Kyrgyzstan.
The book summarises published information on twilight and nocturnal activity, an active season of about 7–8 months and shallow burrows. The species’ biology in Kyrgyzstan is described as unknown.

The book cites published records of spring breeding, gestation of about 26 days and 2–7 embryos. Reports of pregnancy in April come from the Kyzylkum Desert. These figures have not been confirmed for the Kyrgyz population.

The 2006 national account includes the western and northern Tien Shan and the western Fergana Valley in the overall range. The current MDD lists Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan and omits Kyrgyzstan. Current occurrence in Kyrgyzstan has not been established.
The 2006 account describes relatively flat semi-deserts with herbaceous vegetation, ephemeral plants and plants with a short growing season. It also mentions clay sites.

The obtusilobous windflower is a low perennial in the buttercup family. The national book calls it Anemone obtusiloba D.Don. The accepted combination Anemonastrum obtusilobum (D.Don) Mosyakin retains the same nomenclatural type. The change of genus refers to the same species.

According to the 2006 description, the hairy plant reaches about 15 cm. The basal leaves are deeply divided into three parts. The small flowers are pale inside and tinged violet-blue outside. Stony slopes and cliffs in the upper mountain belt, as described in the historical 2006 edition. The national account associates the plant with the high mountains of the Central Tien Shan. These details describe the setting of historical finds and do not map surviving populations today.

The Russian account gives July for flowering. The English summary reports reproduction by seed. No cultivation data were available.

The book lists the Central Tien Shan, the Terskey Ala-Too and the Sary-Jaz basin. No current subspecies is assigned on the basis of these locality records.

The historical account lists development of habitats and unregulated grazing. In 2006, the authors recommended determining the range and population size, establishing a botanical reserve and testing cultivation at the botanical garden.

The national category VU applies to the historical 2006 account and the local conservation unit described there. It is neither a global assessment of the entire current taxon nor a verification of its present legal status. Current population size is unknown, and independent scientific review is pending.
According to the 2006 description, the hairy plant reaches about 15 cm. The basal leaves are deeply divided into three parts. The small flowers are pale inside and tinged violet-blue outside.
The national account associates the plant with the high mountains of the Central Tien Shan. These details describe the setting of historical finds and do not map surviving populations today.
The Russian account gives July for flowering. The English summary reports reproduction by seed. No cultivation data were available.
The book lists the Central Tien Shan, the Terskey Ala-Too and the Sary-Jaz basin. No current subspecies is assigned on the basis of these locality records.
Stony slopes and cliffs in the upper mountain belt, as described in the historical 2006 edition.

The Kashgarian barberry is a spiny high mountain shrub described in the national account as Berberis kaschgarica Rupr. Under the species treatment adopted here from POWO and GBIF, that name falls within Berberis ulicina Hook.f. & Thomson. The national description applies to the historical Kashgarian concept within the broader species.

The Russian account describes a densely branched shrub about 0.5–1 m tall, with three-pronged spines, small leathery leaves and black, broadly oval berries. Stony slopes, old moraines and high plateaux, according to the historical national account. The national source associates the plant with stony high mountain sites and usually records it growing singly. This describes rarity in qualitative terms and provides no current population count.

The account explicitly records reproduction by seed. The Russian and English versions give different flowering and fruiting dates, so precise months were omitted.

For Kyrgyzstan, the 2006 book lists the Sary-Jaz basin in the Central Tien Shan. This national record does not cover the whole current range of B. ulicina.

The historical source names development of the land where it grows as a pressure. In 2006, the authors proposed studying its biology and population size and establishing a reserve where plants are concentrated.

The national category VU applies to the historical 2006 account and the local conservation unit described there. It is neither a global assessment of the entire current taxon nor a verification of its present legal status. Current population size is unknown, and independent scientific review is pending.
The Russian account describes a densely branched shrub about 0.5–1 m tall, with three-pronged spines, small leathery leaves and black, broadly oval berries.
The national source associates the plant with stony high mountain sites and usually records it growing singly. This describes rarity in qualitative terms and provides no current population count.
The account explicitly records reproduction by seed. The Russian and English versions give different flowering and fruiting dates, so precise months were omitted.
For Kyrgyzstan, the 2006 book lists the Sary-Jaz basin in the Central Tien Shan. This national record does not cover the whole current range of B. ulicina.
Stony slopes, old moraines and high plateaux, according to the historical national account.

The large-calyxed primrose is a rosette-forming perennial listed in the 2006 book as Primula macrocalyx Bunge. The subspecies adopted here, Primula veris subsp. macrocalyx (Bunge) Lüdi, is linked directly to the original name in POWO and GRIN. The national conservation unit retains its narrower scope within Primula veris.

The account describes a basal rosette of leaves, a slanting rhizome and an umbel-like inflorescence. The corolla is yellow with orange spots at the base of the lobes. The calyx is inflated and broadly bell-shaped. Forest glades and tall-herb meadows in the forest-meadow belt, as described in the 2006 edition. The book describes local plants as rare and occupying a restricted area. These descriptions give no basis for estimating the number of individuals.

The national account records flowering in May, fruiting in June and reproduction by seed. Current local phenology was not separately verified.

The historical book records the northern slopes of the Kyrgyz Range and the area between the Kegety, Taldy-Bulak and Shamsi rivers. These are historical localities.

The 2006 source names widespread collecting of flowering plants and harvesting for medicinal use. The historical recommendations were to study populations, establish a botanical reserve and test cultivation.

The national category VU applies to the historical 2006 account and the local conservation unit described there. It is neither a global assessment of the entire current taxon nor a verification of its present legal status. Current population size is unknown, and independent scientific review is pending.

The account describes a basal rosette of leaves, a slanting rhizome and an umbel-like inflorescence. The corolla is yellow with orange spots at the base of the lobes. The calyx is inflated and broadly bell-shaped.
The book describes local plants as rare and occupying a restricted area. These descriptions give no basis for estimating the number of individuals.
The national account records flowering in May, fruiting in June and reproduction by seed. Current local phenology was not separately verified.
The historical book records the northern slopes of the Kyrgyz Range and the area between the Kegety, Taldy-Bulak and Shamsi rivers. These are historical localities.
Forest glades and tall-herb meadows in the forest-meadow belt, as described in the 2006 edition.

The coronate spiketail is a large predatory dragonfly in the family Cordulegastridae. The national book uses Sonjagaster coronatus (Morton, 1916). The adopted 2024 revision treats it as Thecagaster coronata (Morton, 1916). Its former placement within Cordulegaster insignis is retained as part of its classification history in the same entry.

The national account describes a large, conspicuous dragonfly. Adult colour and shape should be assessed from identification material, as the former genus name alone is insufficient.
